body: The trachea is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the tubular airway connecting the larynx to the main bronchi. Parameters: (1) the cartilaginous framework — approximately 16-20 C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings, open posteriorly and connected by the trachealis muscle; (2) the mucosal lining — pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells that propel trapped particles upward via the mucociliary escalator; (3) the length and position — approximately 11 cm long in adults, extending from the larynx at the level of C6 vertebra to the carina at T4-T5 where it bifurcates; (4) the blood supply — supplied by the inferior thyroid arteries and drained by the thyroid venous plexus, innervated by the vagus and sympathetic trunks. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, emergency airway management protocols, and thoracic surgery references. e.g.: the trachea described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; tracheostomy tube placement through the anterior tracheal wall in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; tracheal bifurcation visualized on a PA chest radiograph | not: the bronchus (the tubular airway below the tracheal bifurcation, a distinct structure); the larynx (the structure above the trachea housing the vocal folds, a distinct structure) [formal: trachea | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The superior laryngeal nerve is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the branch of the vagus nerve (cranial nerve X) that divides into internal and external divisions to supply the larynx above the level of the vocal folds. Parameters: (1) the origin — arises from the inferior vagal ganglion as the vagus nerve passes the inferior ganglion of the inferior salivary nucleus in the jugular foramen; (2) the internal branch — pierces the thyrohyoid membrane to become the internal laryngeal nerve, providing sensory innervation to the laryngeal mucosa above the vocal folds; (3) the external branch — descends on the inferior pharyngeal constrictor to supply the cricothyroid muscle and the superior laryngeal muscles; (4) the anatomical course — travels with the superior laryngeal artery along the thyrohyoid membrane. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, laryngology references, and regional anesthesia protocols. e.g.: the superior laryngeal nerve described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; superior laryngeal nerve block for laryngeal surgery in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve tested during sensory evaluation of the larynx | not: the recurrent laryngeal nerve (the other laryngeal branch supplying the larynx below the vocal folds); the vagus nerve (the parent nerve from which the superior laryngeal nerve branches, a distinct structure) [formal: nervus laryngeus superior | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The cuneiform cartilage is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the paired nodular elastic cartilages embedded within the substance of the aryepiglottic folds, situated between the corniculate cartilages posteriorly and the lateral margins of the epiglottis anteriorly. Parameters: (1) the position — embedded within the aryepiglottic fold mucosa, lateral to the corniculate cartilage and superior to the arytenoid apex; (2) the composition — elastic cartilage core surrounded by mucous glands and fibroelastic connective tissue; (3) the variability — absent in approximately 25% of individuals (WSN cuneiformis), making its presence a positive anatomical finding on endoscopy; (4) the functional role — stiffens the aryepiglottic fold and contributes to the sphincteric closure of the laryngeal inlet during swallowing. It persists as a standard anatomical variant in human anatomy texts, laryngology atlases, and head and neck radiology. e.g.: the cuneiform cartilage described in Gray's Anatomy, 42nd edition; cuneiform cartilage visible as a nodule on direct laryngoscopy; identification of the cuneiform cartilage on axial CT imaging | not: the corniculate cartilage (sitting atop the arytenoid apex, not embedded in fold mucosa); the aryepiglottic fold (the mucosal fold that contains the cuneiform cartilage, a distinct structure) [formal: cartilago cuneiformis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The vocal ligament is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the free superior margin of the cricothyroid membrane, forming the elastic fiber core of the vocal fold. Parameters: (1) the attachments — anteriorly anchored to the thyroid cartilage at the angle just behind the laryngeal prominence, posteriorly attached to the vocal process of the arytenoid cartilage; (2) the microstructure — densely packed elastic fibers oriented in the anterior-posterior direction, with collagen fibers providing tensile strength; (3) the mucosal covering — the vocal ligament is covered by respiratory epithelium forming the mucosal layer of the vocal fold; (4) the vibratory mechanism — the ligament provides the stiff elastic scaffold upon which the mucosal wave oscillates during phonation. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, laryngology atlases, and voice research protocols. e.g.: the vocal ligament described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; vocal ligament resection in type I thyroplasty for glottic insufficiency; the vocal ligament as the stiff core of the vocal fold in Hirano's structural model of phonation | not: the vocal fold (the entire structure containing the ligament, not just its core); the cricothyroid membrane (the fibrous sheet from which the ligament derives, a distinct structure) [formal: ligamentum vocale | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The cricothyroid membrane is a human-authored anatomical construct mapping the fibrous sheet between the inferior border of the thyroid cartilage and the complete superior border of the cricoid cartilage, forming the floor of the laryngeal cavity and the landmark of the emergency surgical airway. Parameters: (1) the boundaries - superiorly the inferior border of the thyroid laminae, inferiorly the superior border of the cricoid lamina, laterally blending into the cricothyroid joint capsules; (2) the composition - a fibroelastic sheet, thin and transparent anteriorly, with the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve and the superior laryngeal vessels passing on its deep surface; (3) the relationships - its free superior border thickens into the vocal ligament, and the submucosa above it carries the laryngeal mucosa; (4) the clinical access - the site of needle cricothyroidotomy and percutaneous dilational cricothyroidotomy, the standard emergency airway when intubation fails. It persists as a standard anatomical structure in human anatomy texts, emergency airway protocols, and laryngeal surgical planning documents. e.g.: cricothyroid membrane puncture for needle cricothyroidotomy per ATLS 10th edition; the membrane shown in the larynx chapter of Moore Clinically Orientated Anatomy 9th edition; the membrane as the entry point of percutaneous cricothyroidotomy in the ASA difficult airway algorithm | not: the cricoid cartilage (the complete ring forming its inferior border, a distinct structure); the thyrohyoid membrane (the membrane above it between thyroid and hyoid); the cricothyroid joint (the articulation between the cartilages, lateral to the membrane) [formal: membrana cricothyroidea | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The arytenoid cartilage is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the paired pyramidal cartilages forming the posterior anchor of the vocal fold apparatus within the laryngeal framework. Parameters: (1) the shape — a pyramidal cartilage with a base articulating with the cricoid lamina and an apex directed superiorly; (2) the vocal process — an anterior projection serving as the posterior attachment of the vocal fold; (3) the muscular process — a lateral projection serving as the insertion point for intrinsic laryngeal muscles; (4) the articular facet — a smooth surface articulating with the cricoid cartilage to enable rotation and sliding of the arytenoids. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, laryngology atlases, and airway management guidelines. e.g.: the arytenoid cartilage described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; arytenoid cartilage displacement visible on lateral neck radiograph; arytenoid cartilage repositioning surgery for unilateral vocal fold paralysis in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition | not: the corniculate cartilage (a smaller cartilage sitting atop the arytenoid apex); the cricoarytenoid joint (the articulation between the arytenoid and cricoid cartilages, a distinct structure) [formal: cartilago arytenoidea | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The laryngeal ventricle is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the hourglass-shaped recess between the superior (vestibular) folds and inferior (vocal) folds within the laryngeal cavity. Parameters: (1) the boundaries — anteriorly and posteriorly it extends as the laryngeal saccule, a blind pouch that can become distended; medially bounded by the vocal folds inferiorly and vestibular folds superiorly; (2) the mucosal lining — stratified squamous epithelium continuous with the mucosa of both the ventricular and vocal folds; (3) the laryngeal saccule — a vertical pouch extending superiorly from the anterior portion of the ventricle, containing mucous glands and occasionally distended in laryngoceles; (4) the functional significance — the ventricle serves as a space for the free vibration of the vocal fold mucosa, unencumbered by the overlying vestibular fold. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, laryngology atlases, and airway management references. e.g.: the laryngeal ventricle described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; laryngocele arising from distension of the laryngeal saccule in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; visualization of the laryngeal ventricle during indirect laryngoscopy | not: the laryngeal vestibule (the chamber above the vocal folds from the inlet to the folds, a distinct space); the vocal fold (the mucosal structure forming the inferior boundary of the ventricle, a distinct structure) [formal: ventriculus laryngis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The laryngeal inlet is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the opening connecting the oropharynx to the laryngeal vestibule. Parameters: (1) the boundaries — anteriorly bounded by the epiglottis, laterally by the aryepiglottic folds, and posteriorly by the arytenoid cartilages; (2) the spatial orientation — angled approximately 45 degrees downward in the upright position, directing the food bolus around the epiglottis and into the esophagus; (3) the protective mechanism — the epiglottis tilts posteriorly and the aryepiglottic folds contract inward during swallowing to close the inlet and protect the airway; (4) the clinical access — the laryngeal inlet is the target of direct and video laryngoscopy for endotracheal intubation, visualized as the dark opening between the epiglottis and the arytenoid cartilages. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, emergency airway management protocols, and laryngology references. e.g.: the laryngeal inlet described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; laryngeal inlet visualization during direct laryngoscopy in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition; the laryngeal inlet as the target of rapid sequence intubation in emergency medicine | not: the glottis (the region below the laryngeal inlet containing the vocal folds); the laryngeal vestibule (the chamber within the larynx above the vocal folds, a distinct space) [formal: aditus laryngis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]

The rima glottidis is a human-authored anatomical construct that maps the slit-like opening between the vocal folds and their processes within the glottis. Parameters: (1) the boundaries — anteriorly bounded by the space between the vocal processes of the arytenoid cartilages, posteriorly by the space between the body of the arytenoid cartilages; (2) the functional states — widened to the triangle of the respiratory rima during breathing (abducted vocal folds), narrowed to the slit of phonation during voiced speech (adducted vocal folds), and fully closed during coughing and Valsalva; (3) the measurement — approximately 10 mm in length and 3-4 mm in width during quiet breathing in adults; (4) the clinical significance — the narrowest dimension of the rima glottidis determines the airflow resistance during phonation and the minimum endotracheal tube size that can pass through an adducted airway. It persists as a standard anatomical landmark in human anatomy texts, laryngology, and airway management guidelines. e.g.: the rima glottidis described in Moore Clinically Oriented Anatomy, 9th edition; measurement of the rima glottidis during laryngeal electromyography; the rima glottidis evaluated by stroboscopy in Cummings Otolaryngology, 6th edition | not: the glottis (the entire anatomical region including the vocal folds and rima, not just the opening); the laryngeal inlet (the opening to the larynx above the vocal folds, a distinct structure) [formal: rima glottidis | substrate: mind | horizon: as-long-as-us | explicit: yes]
